topic_alignment.paraphrase: The lecturer recaps proposer, solver and verifier roles, then mentions supplying proposers with textbooks or examples. Page 6 supplies R-Zero and Absolute Zero prompt screenshots related to this recap. The available captions do not separately read these prompts or establish a distinct page-6 transition. This contextual range intentionally overlaps the page-5 range used in chapter 14.

An AI agent contains at least a harness and a language model. The lecturer recalls the language-model updating discussed earlier. On this slide, the flame icon is inside the language-model component; the harness is labelled lowercase h and the language-model parameters theta.

The lecturer asks whether the harness, as another component of an AI agent, can also be updated continuously. In the otherwise repeated diagram, the flame icon moves from the language-model component to the harness component.

Agent behavior depends on both language-model parameters theta and its harness h. The lecture distinguishes the human-desired target L-hat from a defined proxy loss L, and describes replacing h by a candidate h-prime in hopes of lower loss. The gradient-like update on the slide has a red question mark: the lecturer says a harness can be difficult even to parameterize, so differentiating the loss with respect to it is not straightforward. The printed loss is L(A_{theta,h}, H), with uppercase H still denoting human-provided information.

A language model can propose a revised harness from the existing harness code and its evaluation score. The proposer may be the evolving model itself or a separate fixed module. The internally defined benchmark or loss is not necessarily the human-desired final loss. Candidate generation and iteration are described as a possible improvement process, not a guarantee of held-out improvement.
